subject: pixelDungeonProps
pitch:
Category: Prop group.
Subject: dungeon props: chest, torches, barrels, bones, spike trap.
Style: pixel art.
reasoning:
I'm planning a dungeon prop group—chest, torches, barrels, bones, spike trap—in pixel art style using the pixel kit, aiming for a rich but robust build with around 200+ parts and multiple textures since props don't require joints like a character would.

To be safe I'll create a single root joint at the origin so every part has somewhere to attach. I'm sketching out the layout: a stone-tiled dungeon floor slab with a large chest centered toward the back, designed with its lid tilted open at roughly 35 degrees to reveal a glowing gold interior.

Working out the hinge math for the lid...

For sub-decorations attached to the lid, like the metal bands, I also need a helper that maps a local point relative to the hinge into world space using the same rotation, so parts rotate together consistently when the lid opens. For the chest's visual style I'm planning pixel-art textures for wood planks and iron bands using a tiled voxel approach with a fixed texel size.

I'm settling on a texel size around 0.03m generally, with finer 0.015m detail for the chest. For the floor, I'm building it from individual flagstone tiles arranged in a grid with slight random height variation and gaps for mortar, so nothing floats and props sit cleanly at a fixed floor height of 0.12.

Now I'm laying out the scene footprint at 2.8×2.0: the hero chest sits back-center-left, flanked by two tall standing torch braziers at the back corners to establish height, while a cluster of three barrels (two upright, one on its side) fills the right-back area, aiming for a pixel-art octagonal barrel silhouette.

I'm figuring out how to paint the barrel wood staves and iron hoops using cell-based coloring tied to UV parity and local height, since lathe geometry doesn't take textures directly.

For the hoop bands I'll add actual extra geometry — slim cylinders slightly wider than the barrel body at specific heights — and I'm shaping the barrel body's lathe profile with points curving outward from the axis and back in, careful not to let the outline self-intersect.

I'm planning three distinct barrels: one closed with a lid, one open showing a glowing green liquid inside, and one lying on its side using a horizontal lathe axis, resting against the floor.

For the paint function on the lying barrel, I realize the lathe's `s` parameter already gives height along axis and degrees around it, which is exactly what I need for hoop and stave stripes.

Staves alternate shade based on angular segment parity, with hoops determined by height ranges, and I can quantize height into texel-sized bands for pixelation. For wood grain texture I'll use the kit's bayer dithering function on the quantized height and stave index to add subtle tonal variation.

I'm checking that texel density on painted areas like barrels is fine enough for the 0.03m cell grid, while bones and other simple shapes can just use flat varied tones from a limited bone-colored palette rather than full texture painting.

Now I'm designing a spike trap near the front: a 0.9×0.9 pressure plate framed by border boxes, with a recessed dark pit and a 4×4 grid of pyramidal spikes of varying heights emerging from it, plus bloodstains and scattered bones nearby for detail.

Working out the tip cone's radius and vertical position so it exactly caps the spike's taper, scaled slightly larger for the bloody overlay effect. I'm also considering adding a warning rune decal, like a pixel-art skull texture on a plane oriented to face upward on the floor in front of the trap.

For the torches, I'm deciding to skip a full back wall and instead use two standing iron torch posts as the tallest props in the scene, since the subject needs to remain the tallest element overall.

Designing torch flame geometry...

I want glow to work on textured cards so each flame reads its own pixel-art colors, plus a solid glowing core box and a few tiny ember specks scattered nearby for extra flicker. For the stand itself, I'm thinking a stone plinth base, wood post, iron collar rings, and a lathe-turned brazier bowl on top holding glowing coals beneath the flame.

Then I'll add a dropped, unlit hand-torch on the floor near the chest as a third small prop—just a short charred stick lying on its side. Now I'm working out the final scene layout: floor dimensions and tile grid, torch positions flanking the chest, and the chest's own placement and rotation as the focal point.

To keep things simple, I'll decide against rotating the chest or torches—applying yaw would require a more complex local-to-world transform helper, and since the chest lid already needs an X rotation for opening, adding yaw on top would need quaternions rather than simple Euler angles. So I'll leave the chest and torches axis-aligned, letting barrels (which are rotationally symmetric anyway) and other smaller props carry any variation instead.

Now I'm working out positions for the torches and barrels so they don't overlap—checking the distance between a torch at (1.15, -0.75) and a nearby barrel against their combined radii. I'm roughly placing an upright barrel, an open barrel, and a lying barrel near the front-right, then setting the chest's footprint at center (-0.2, -0.35) with dimensions about 0.95 wide by 0.6 deep, with its lid hinge along the back edge.

Moving the torch to (1.25,-0.8) clears the plinth collision since the nearest distance now exceeds 0.32, and the plinth edge stays within the floor bounds. Now I'm placing a lying barrel C on the left side around (-1.05, 0.0).

I'm checking the barrel's lathe orientation along z and adjusting its x-position to -1.1 so its extent doesn't touch the chest, then verifying its z-range stays clear of the left torch's plinth zone — the gap works out fine without rotation.

Now I'm placing the spike trap at front center-right and checking it against barrel B's extent; there's a tiny overlap at x .73-.75 so I nudge the trap center to (0.2, 0.62), clearing the left side. I'm also scattering bones — a skull, ribcage, and femur near the spike trap suggesting an impaled skeleton victim, plus considering a skull resting atop the barrel.

For the femur I'm using a shaft box with knuckle blobs at each end, and for the skull a cranium box with jaw, eye sockets, and a pixel-art textured plane for the teeth/face detail on the front. The ribcage I'm building from a spine box with curved rib pairs, possibly low-poly torus arcs rotated into place to suggest a half-buried skeleton.

Working out rib orientation: since the spine runs along z, the rib arches sit naturally in the XY plane using the torus's default orientation, so I'm spacing six ribs along the spine with shrinking radius, flattened to lie against the floor, plus small vertebrae boxes and a pelvis, with extra scattered femurs and arm bones nearby.

Now I'm positioning the skeleton toward the left-front, running the spine along z with the rib cage, pelvis, and skull laid out front-to-back so the skull faces the viewer while the femurs extend forward past the ribs toward the floor edge.

Fixing the skull orientation since a skeleton lying on its back should face upward rather than forward, so I'm adjusting the rotation about the x-axis to tip the face toward the ceiling while keeping it readable to the viewer.

Now I'm sketching the chest details: planked wooden body with a lid, plus adding a second skull resting on top of the barrel for set dressing.

For the chest hardware, I'm designing a stepped lid profile with a lower box and smaller top box for that pixel-art roof look, then adding vertical iron straps across body and lid, corner brackets, a front lock plate with keyhole and gold accent, side ring handles, and tiny rivet studs along the bands.

For the small repeated pieces like studs and nails, I'll merge their geometries by color/bone using BufferGeometryUtils to stay within a reasonable part budget, aiming for 180-340 parts total. Inside, I'm planning a dark hollow interior with a glowing pile of gold coins and colored gem boxes rising above the body's top edge to simulate overflowing treasure.

Instead of a solid top, I'll build the chest as four plank walls plus a bottom floor, with a red cloth lining plane on the inside floor, then stack gold coin boxes on top rising toward 0.38 height.

Stacking the gold heap layers...

I'll scatter a few spilled coins outside the chest on the floor and give the pile and coins a subtle gold glow to sell the treasure feel. I'm also thinking about an iron lock plate and hasp on the lid front, but I'll skip the hasp for simplicity.

Now I'm working out the lid geometry: wooden plank texture with iron rim trim, hinged at the back at a 38° open angle, with the lid's local box dimensions split into a base and top panel plus iron straps positioned near the edges and center to reinforce the look.

I'm writing a helper function that computes each lid piece's world position by rotating its local coordinates around the hinge point using a standard rotation formula, so parts swing open correctly together.

For textures, I'm planning a small set covering wood planks with nail details, iron plating with rivets, cracked mossy stone flagstones, a gold coin pattern, and a skull face design.

I'm also sketching out several more textures -- flames, a keyhole plate, a warning rune decal, vertical wood grain for posts, a grated iron trap plate, a dithered bone tile, a glowing slime texture for barrel liquid, and glowing coals for a brazier, aiming for a good variety using the pixel kit's random seed utilities to drive the detail generation.

Now I'm working out a deterministic noise helper and a plank texture: defining a wood color ramp, then laying out rows with seams, highlights, grain dither, randomized butt joints, and nail details to make the planks feel hand-placed rather than uniform.

Writing hash function...

Still writing plank texture logic...

Face height becomes 11.4 px with those scaled texels, which creates inconsistent sizing across faces, so I'll widen the tile to 64px to keep the wood texel at a clean 0.02 scale, giving 1.28m at that resolution.

I'm setting a general texel of 0.02 across chest, floor, and other items, with floor tiles at 0.5m mapping to 25 texels using a 32×32 tile texture, while smaller items like coins and bones get their own finer texel. For the iron tile I'm designing a 16×16 pixel texture with a dithered dark steel base, lighter highlights on the top and left edges, darker shading on the bottom and right, and a rivet detail in the center, sized so the iron strap width maps cleanly onto a cropped section of that tile.

Now I'm refining the iron texel to 0.015 for a 6px strap width, then moving to the flagstone tile: a 32×32 stone texture with dithered ramps, mortar borders, per-stone edge highlighting, random cracks, and mossy green accents, mapped onto the tile box faces with randomized offsets for variety. I'm also sketching out a 16×16 gold coin pattern with staggered circular coins, each shaded with a base tone, darker ring outline, and a bright highlight pixel.

Now I'm designing a 12×12 pixel skull face using bone-light, shadow, and dark-outline characters to lay out the cranium, eye sockets, and nose shape row by row.

I'm simplifying the approach to use two separate boxes for the skull—a cranium box and a jaw box—each with its own face texture, so I can keep the eyes/nose pattern separate from the teeth pattern rather than cramming everything into one texture.

For coloring, I'm defining a bone palette with light, shadow, and dark tones, then planning to generate a small dithered bone-colored texture I can reuse across all the skeletal pieces like the skull, femurs, and ribs for subtle surface variation instead of flat solid colors.

Now I'm sketching a flame texture as a small pixel grid, laying out rows of characters to represent red, orange, yellow, and white-hot pixels that taper into a flickering flame shape.

Beyond the flame, I'm thinking through card placement details—orientation, lean, cross-billboard flow for visibility from multiple angles, and sizing—then I'm drawing a smaller keyhole plate texture with a gold rim and dark keyhole center using the same row-based pixel grid approach.

For the trap rune decal, I'm sketching a 16x16 pixel skull-and-crossbones warning mark in red-brown tones to signal danger on the floor, working out the outline and eye cutouts row by row.

Still writing pixelArt rows...

Switching to the trap plate texture: a dark iron grate with a 4x4 hole grid for spikes to emerge from, darker spike holes, and riveted corners, sized to align with the spike spacing.

Since the top face UV matches the x-axis symmetrically, there's no orientation issue there. For the other textures, I'm planning a 16×16 slime texture with dithered greens and lighter bubbles plus a glow, an 8×8 coal texture with orange-black embers and glow, and an 8×32 post texture using vertical wood grain filled column by column.

Working through the texel sizing for the post's side faces, I'm calculating that the fit factor needs to scale up significantly since the height-to-texel ratio exceeds the texture's resolution—so I'm adjusting the tile dimensions to something like 8×72 to keep the texel size consistent across faces.

Now for the brazier, I'm designing the iron bowl as a lathe shape with an 8-segment profile, trying to figure out a point sequence that forms a solid cup shape with a flat rim rather than crossing itself. I'm settling on a simple solid bowl profile that flares outward to a flat top, then planning to add separate coal-pile geometry sitting above the rim to simulate glowing embers.

Then I work out a thin ring profile for the rim lip using overlapping radii, and plan a short cylinder with a coal/glow texture sitting inside that ring, with flame billboard cards placed just above it to complete the brazier effect.

Now I'm designing the torch post structure: a stone plinth base with a stepped upper tier, a tall post with iron collar bands at intervals, and diagonal iron braces connecting post to plinth for support, plus a scatter of tiny glowing ember cubes floating above the flames for extra detail.

For the floor glow beneath torches, I could use a pixel-art dithered light pool texture with concentric orange rings and a checker-style alpha pattern instead of a smooth gradient, keeping it flat-colored but stylistically consistent with the pixel aesetic.

I'm also sketching a small unlit hand torch prop—stick plus charred head—placed near the trap area, and starting to lay out the spike trap's frame geometry with stone border pieces.

Working out the trap plate dimensions and the spike cones, sizing the border so a 0.72 plate fits inside a 0.9 outer frame, then setting cone radius and segment count so the spikes read as axis-aligned pyramids.

Now I'm varying spike heights across the array for an "armed" look, with most tall and a few short stubs, and assigning steel coloring with some blood-red tips for visual variety, using flat shading on the low-poly cones.

I'm adding small iron collar boxes around each spike base for detail, then placing stud boxes on the frame corners. I need to reposition the trap closer to center since the floor rune decal in front of it would otherwise overflow past the floor's edge.

I'm shifting the chest further back to z around -0.4 to give the trap more room, keeping the torches and barrel positions clear. Rather than cramming a warning glyph right at the trap's front edge, I'm considering widening the floor depth to 2.4 to make space.

Now I'm working out the tile grid layout: six columns by four rows, each tile roughly 0.48 by 0.58 with small gaps, and slight height variation around 0.1-0.12 so props resting on top stay at a consistent level. I want a dark mortar base peeking through the gaps between tiles for texture.

I'll add a dark underlay box beneath gaps for mortar visibility, plus a few small rubble boxes for broken tile chips, skipping crates or cobwebs for now. For barrels, I'm defining each one with a lathed body, barrel paint, and two hoops.

Still computing barrel profile...

I'm worried about alignment between the lathe octagon and the hoop cylinder octagon — if they're rotated relative to each other, the hoop's inner corners might poke through the barrel's flat faces at the midpoint radius. I should just make the hoop radius a bit larger (like 1.06x) to stay safely outside regardless of rotation offset.

For the hoops themselves, I'll stick with separate geometry rather than trying to paint them onto the texture, since geometry hoops would hide painted ones anyway — paint can be reserved for the stave lines. For the barrel top, I'm considering a small flat cylinder disc as a lid, textured to match the planks.

Shaping the lid texture now with plank stripes and a ring border, plus a small dark bung hole detail. For the open barrel variant, I'm working out a lathe profile that includes an inner wall so the barrel reads as hollow, adjusting the inner radius points so they stay smaller than the outer wall without crossing it.

I'm sizing the liquid cylinder inside the barrel so its octagonal cross-section hides just inside the inner wall, nudging the radius down slightly so the vertices don't poke through visibly. Now I'm drafting the barrel paint function, which needs different top-face logic depending on whether the barrel is standing upright or lying on its side.

For the lathe shape, I'm using the height parameter to detect the two end caps versus the side surface, then applying plank-style striping by quantizing position along different axes depending on orientation -- since a lying barrel's ends face along z rather than y, the stripe pattern needs to use x and z coordinates instead of just x.

For distinguishing inner from outer barrel walls, I'll pass the barrel's center point into the factory function and compute horizontal distance from that center, since the inner surface sits at a smaller radius than the outer stave surface at the same height.

I'm skipping the closed lying barrel for now and keeping center-passing just for vertical ones. For the stave coloring, I'm bucketing by angle into 8 sectors, giving each a ramped base tone via a hash function, adding grain dithering quantized along height, and darkening near stave boundaries to simulate seams -- then feeding that into a wood palette picker with dithering.

Now I'm moving on to writing the bone geometry code, starting with the femur.

Writing bone frame helpers...

Still designing the box helper type...

I'm checking whether the texture colors count as "colored" versus greyscale -- comparing max-min channel differences for bone (warm tan) and iron (bluish gray) to decide if tinting applies.

I also need to track the flat color budget across all parts: white, bone tones, steel, blood, dark, gold, gems, cloth, coin colors, etc. -- staying well under the 64 distinct color limit, probably under 30 total.

Glow works fine on textured parts since it clones the material, and glow accepts either a single part's mesh or an array of meshes like card groups. For parts without an explicit bone assignment, they attach to the nearest joint, which defaults to root at the origin since that's the only joint defined.

I'll explicitly pass bone anyway to keep positioning rigid and predictable. Now I'm sketching the module imports, pulling in the builder, frame, rng helpers, and deciding to define my own degree-to-radian constant rather than rely on an uncertain DEG export, plus importing pixelArt, pixelTexture, tileBox, pick, bayer, and the glow kit.

Defining color palettes...

Adding crack details to the stone texture...

Finishing the iron texture with rivet highlights, then starting the gold coin texture using row-based offsets to create a coin-stack pattern.

Still writing skull pixel grid...

Verifying row widths all come out to 12, then moving to designing the teeth grid, sketching a basic 8x3 pattern to try out.

Still mapping out the flame grid pixel rows...

Continuing the row-by-row character count verification, each checks out against the expected width of 12. Now I'm shifting to designing the 8×10 keyhole shape, setting up a palette of colors for the gradient highlights and shadows.

Still writing keyhole grid...

Now I'm defining the slime palette with light bubble highlights, a coal grid cycling through ember colors, and a wood post texture with vertical grain streaks based on noise functions.

I'm also planning the trap plate, a glyph rune decal, and mossy stone textures, then setting up the dungeon props builder with a root joint and helper functions for creating boxes and cylinders attached to that joint.

Now I'm laying out the floor with a dark base slab and a grid of stone tiles, computing tile dimensions and spacing so five columns and four rows of 0.47-wide tiles with small gaps cover the full 3.0×2.4 floor area, using a hash function to randomly vary tile heights slightly for a worn look.

I'm adding scattered rubble boxes for detail, then starting to define the chest prop with fixed footprint and height constants, beginning with a plinth skirt underlay slightly wider than the chest body.

Still writing chest geometry...

Still stacking heap layers...

Now I'm placing jeweled accents on top of the heap—small rotated cubes for ruby, sapphire, and emerald gems sitting near the top edge, plus I'm sketching iron strap boxes running vertically down the front and sides of the body.

Working out corner brackets and reinforcement bands next: I'm testing a wraparound ring band at mid-height but it overlaps the straps, so I'm switching to angle-iron corner brackets at all four vertical edges instead, then adding a small lock plate detail.

Now I'm figuring out the lock assembly layering: an iron plate on the front face, a gold lock body on top of it, and a keyhole cutout plane sitting just in front of both, computing exact z-offsets so each layer sits flush against the wall surface and straps without clipping through.

I'm also adding side handle loops as rotated torus shapes with anchor plates, plus small cube studs along the front straps for decoration, before shifting focus to defining the lid's hinge point and local coordinate frame.

For the lid itself, I'm building wood-plank base and top sections plus stepped end caps, and placing iron straps across the lid at matching x-positions to the body straps for visual continuity.

Then I'm adding a front iron lip at the lid edge and hinge barrel cylinders rotated to lie along the x-axis at the lid's pivot points, positioned so they align with the hinge geometry regardless of lid rotation.

I'm writing a coordinate transform function that maps local lid-space points into world space by applying the lid's opening angle as a rotation about the X axis, checking that when the angle is zero (closed) the transform reduces correctly to the base position.

Working through the geometry, I'm computing the lid's maximum height and back extent when open, accounting for the thickness offset and the hinge rotation pushing the lid's edges forward and slightly behind the hinge line.

Now I'm placing six small gold coin discs scattered on the floor in front of the chest, keeping them between the chest's front edge and avoiding overlap with the skull prop, and giving them a subtle glow.

For the barrels, I'm positioning three: one closed with a skull resting on top near one corner, one open with slime nearby, and a third tipped over on its side using a rotated lathe axis so it lies flush with the floor — checking that its radius doesn't cause clipping below the ground plane.

I'm adding hoop rings around each barrel at varying heights for detail, matching the curve of each barrel's radius, plus thinking about a small "poison" label plane with a skull-and-bone graphic curved onto the open barrel's front facet, positioning it carefully so it doesn't clip through the octagonal geometry.

I'll decide on decal designs instead: a green skull tag for poison and a red X-in-circle brand mark, both generated as small pixel textures. Then I'm moving on to positioning a lying skeleton figure at the base, setting up a local frame with slight yaw to place the spine and skull.

Working out spine and rib geometry...

Skipping the sternum since it'd intersect the ribs, I'll add clavicle boxes instead, then build the pelvis from a central block plus two angled iliac blades, and extend femurs and tibias outward from the pelvis at calculated yaw angles and positions.

Checking the full skeleton length, the legs extend too far down, so I'm shortening the spine and legs and re-centering the skeleton to avoid the skull colliding with the chest geometry, nudging the x-position to maintain clearance.

I'm splaying the femurs outward and angling the tibias back to keep the legs within the floor bounds, then shifting the trap's center rightward to avoid overlapping the skeleton, and rechecking the barrel's position against the trap's extent.

I'm nudging barrel B and figure A further apart to clear the minimum distance threshold, verifying each shape's bounding radius against the trap's rim, and considering shrinking the trap's outer diameter if the tangent overlap at x=0.8 remains too tight.

Shifting focus to the trap's actual geometry, I'm placing it at plate radius 0.64 with an 0.08 border for an outer size of 0.8, centered so it spans roughly x -0.1 to 0.7 and z 0.15 to 0.95, then working out pixel offsets for the spike holes so the 4x4 grid sits symmetrically with enough gap between cone bases. I also check the skeleton's position and spread against the trap boundary, and verify the skull's world-space z-coordinate clears the chest piece after accounting for the figure's local origin offset.

Checking the pelvis and femur extents, then moving the torch-holding hand to a position that stays clear of the trap's z-range and the skeleton's leg spread. I'm now worried the spike tops plus the skeleton's height could occlude the chest's lower body from a straight front view, so I'm weighing whether shifting the trap further to the right keeps the chest fully visible as the hero piece.

Trying a revised layout: shifting the chest's center to the left, repositioning the torches outward, and adjusting the barrels and trap positions so their footprints don't overlap the chest or each other, checking distances between each pair to confirm clearance.

Adjusting trap bounds against B still shows a slight corner overlap, so I'm nudging B to (1.15,-0.12), which clears it with a safe margin. Now checking B against the torch plinth position next.

Then I'm sizing the floor glyph—slightly overflowing the floor limit, so I'm expanding the floor depth to 2.6 with four tile rows at 0.65 spacing, recalculating tile centers and torch z-positions accordingly. Now I'm placing the left skeleton and a lying barrel prop, working out their bounding boxes relative to the room layout.

Then I'm resolving the floor width conflict by adjusting to 5 columns of 0.64 tiles (3.2 total width), recomputing centers and confirming torch placement and texel resolution fit within limits. I'm also placing an unlit hand torch and planning a scattered bone pile—skull and femur—near the trap.

Now I'm sketching out the skull helper function, defining its position, rotation order, and multi-part composite origin for proper orientation.

Still writing rig helper...

Writing the tile box helper function...

Writing import statements and setup code...

I'm deciding to move texture and palette generation inside the build function as closures so everything stays deterministic and fresh per build call, rather than creating them at module load time.

Now I'm working out the torch prop geometry—placing a stone plinth, upper platform, post, and collars at stacked heights above the floor, with the bowl positioned at the top of the post.

Still writing bowl geometry...

Positioning the coal glow near the top of the rim, then layering flame cards above it with varying sizes and slight offsets for a flickering look, plus scattering small glowing ember boxes around the flame area.

I'm also planning a tiny decorative skull mounted on the post, building a reusable skull helper function that constructs the cranium and jaw from boxes relative to a bottom-center origin.

Finishing the cranium with a textured face plane sized to match a 12x10 skull-face texture, positioned flush against the front of the box with the correct orientation.

Setting the cranium height to 0.15 so the plane fits proportionally, then working out the jaw's dimensions and placement so it sits slightly recessed beneath the cranium overhang, with a teeth texture plane matched to the jaw's front face.

I'm also planning glowing eye sockets for the skull, positioning small boxes within the face texture grid to calculate where left and right eye coordinates fall relative to the plane's width and height.

Setting eyes slightly in front of the plane face so they're visible. Now I'm defining a reusable bone function: a cylindrical shaft along the z-axis with bone-colored material, plus hexagonal knob caps at both ends offset symmetrically for the joint bulges.

For ribs I'm using a torus geometry arched in a half-circle, flattened and scaled to give it a curved rib shape, with a light bone tint and flat shading. I'm now assembling the full skeleton with a slight yaw rotation applied through the rig.

For skull placement, I'm setting up a separate rig offset from the body position with additional yaw and a steep pitch tilt. I'm also now building a spike trap structure: a rectangular frame made of four stone beams positioned along the edges, topped with a flat plate piece.

Adding corner studs and spikes...

Still adding plate details...

I'm reconsidering the lowered-tile logic to avoid unwanted gaps—maybe restrict it to just the far corner tiles so nothing floats awkwardly, checking where the glyph tile's x-position actually lands among the five column centers.

Actually, simpler to skip lowered tiles entirely and get visual variety through texture cracks and scattered rubble boxes instead. Writing barrel position coordinates...

Writing barrel and hoop geometry code...

Actually I'll use a dithered cell-paint function for the hoops to get that pixel-art alternation look, picking iron shades with slight brightness variation based on normal direction. Keeping the barrel cylinders closed since the interior won't be visible, except where the barrel opening is cut.

For barrel A, I'll place a small skull decoration near the top rim. For the lying barrel C, I'm rotating its cylinder axis to align with Z instead of the default Y, using a quaternion from an Euler rotation so the hoops and planks wrap correctly around the horizontal orientation.

I'm deciding to skip adding a tap spigot and wedge chocks under barrel C to keep things simpler, and moving on to building the hand torch with a wooden stick post as its base.

Now I'm detailing the torch head: a charred wood block with cloth wrap bands around it, making sure the whole torch lies flat with its bottom resting on the floor. I'm skipping extra loose items like potions and candles, and instead scattering a few rubble piles at different positions using small stone blocks.

I'll scatter a handful of small stone rubble pieces, skip cobwebs for now, and add a bone pile near the barrel with a femur and a second skull positioned nearby. I'm deciding against chains or shackles, and planning glow effects on gold, gems, coins, flames, coals, embers, slime, skull eyes, and a dim red glowing rune glyph on the floor for a nice trap effect.

Now I'm tallying up the total piece count across the whole scene: roughly 23 for the floor and rubble, about 65 for the chest with its straps, studs, lid details, and coin pile, around 54 for both torches combined, 30 for the three barrels, 49 for the trap with its spikes and glyph, and about 58 for the skeleton's skull, spine, ribs, and limb bones.

Adding in the loose bones and the hand torch, I'm landing on a total around 290 pieces. Then I'm counting up distinct textures needed -- planks, iron, stone, gold, bone, skull face, teeth, flame, keyhole, slime, coals, post, trap plate, glyph, poison, brand -- that's 16, which should fit comfortably in an atlas since each one is small.

I'm writing the barrel paint function for the lid and cap faces, checking the height to detect end caps and generating a plank-like pattern with edge highlighting based on position.

For the open barrel's interior, I'm working out the logic so the rim annulus still reads as planks while the inner walls get a darker, wetter wood tone, making sure the inside-wall check only fires when the normal isn't pointing straight up so it doesn't clash with the rim.

Now I'm writing the stave segmentation logic, dividing the barrel's circumference into 45-degree sections to drive the vertical plank seams.

Still writing stave texture...

I'm estimating the total painted surface area across the barrels, hoops, and bowl to gauge texture density, landing around 8 square meters combined.

Now I'm working on a floor glyph texture using a small pixel grid to draw a crossbones-and-skull warning symbol, sketching out the diagonal line segments and skull shape before simplifying the approach.

Still writing pixel-drawing code...

Designing the poison label as a 12x12 pixel grid with a green background, dark border, and a white skull pattern drawn with row strings...

Now I'm sketching the 10×10 brand icon, a red circle with an X, and thinking it'd be simpler to generate it programmatically based on distance from center to create the ring shape.

For decal placement I need to position it on or near the surface with proper direction and size. I also want a 16×16 slime texture with greens and bubble highlights, and need to confirm the glow effect only applies to standard materials that aren't the paint material.

For card frames I'm checking that frame() accepts a position array and optional direction/up vectors, and that cards() returns an array of meshes compatible with glow(). I need to verify alphaTest is preserved through cloning, size flame cards to match their texture aspect ratio, and make sure glow correctly handles emissive maps on textured parts without breaking the atlas texture.

Now I'm figuring out the chest wall plank tiling and offsets, building the lid parts using a pitch rotation for the opening angle, and defining small stud details with their positions along the front and lid straps.

Scattering coins across the chest floor with varied positions, including a leaning stack of three, using flat gold cylinder geometry stacked slightly apart in height; placing a skeleton skull off to the side and starting to size a ruby gem for a treasure box.

Now I'm setting up a helper function for placing rig parts, handling quaternion rotation composition and optional texture/scale/flat-shading parameters, while thinking through the typing for color/paint arguments.

Writing the Rig class...

Adding a helper for long bones that computes a rig transform from a local offset and builds the bone mesh at the given length, with the rig origin centered on the bone and offset slightly above the floor.

Now I'm defining shaft knobs on the ends, picking a flat bone color, and setting up a sequential seed generator for texture variation.
